query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: The unique design concept of HEAs can be applied to the innovation of a new generation of powder superalloys and the development of turbine disk components suitable for the extreme working conditions of the aero-engine. Combining MA (mechanical alloying) with SPS (spark plasma sintering) to prepare HEAs has recently received much attention. MA overcomes phase diagram limitations by using mechanical energy to effect the atomic alloying of solid components, producing alloy systems inaccessible to conventional procedures and increasing powder homogeneity and solid solubility. SPS is a new rapid sintering technology commonly used to prepare high-performance HEA blocks. It combines plasma activation and hot-pressing sintering and benefits from fast heating and cooling rates, short sintering times, controllable microstructures, energy savings, and low environmental impact. Pulse current heating and high pressure can rapidly heat and sinter the powder particles into sintered blocks [,,]. CrMnFeCoNi alloy can be fabricated by either casting (melting and solidification) [,,,], sintering (powder metallurgy) [,,,], or other methods [,,,,]. Compared with the more frequently studied casting, sintering has a great economic advantage in saving materials and energy []. On the other hand, the element distribution in sintered alloys is usually more inhomogeneous than that of casted ones. One example is the Cr, Mn, and O enrichment in spark-plasma-sintered alloys []. The zones with specific element enrichment generally affect the mechanical properties and electrochemical stability. In addition, the impurities of carbon or oxygen from raw powders also play essential roles in the above properties. Therefore, the relationship between the specific microstructure, the mechanical properties, and the electrochemical stability of sintered alloys needs to be sufficiently clarified. Furthermore, AM processing with mechanically alloyed powder is problematic because the highly deformed powders have poor flow and, thus, reduced feedstock delivery properties. Studies have also shown that powder shape and size distribution contribute significantly to the quality of AM builds. Mechanical and microstructural analysis confirm the success this new fabrication pathway had in creating dispersion strengthened metallic alloys.

Casting [] and powder metallurgy [] are two common methods for preparing HEAs. For casting, there are two kinds of defects which are the vaporization of low melting-point elements and the elements segregation in the ingot []. For powder metallurgy, the HEAs can be prepared by MA and then consolidated. The HEAs powders prepared by MA are uniform and fine, and even form nanocrystalline. Hence a rapid sintering is needed to maintain this microstructure []. SPS is a new field-assisted sintering technique which can effectively suppress the grain coarsening by rapid heating and efficient densification in a few minutes [,,]. Compared with MA, gas atomization can produce more homogeneous powders. decision.trend: Researchers have been exploring various methods to create uniform W-Cu materials, including spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, and vapor-coated W powders. Despite these efforts, phase separation, void formation, and defects remain significant challenges. Recent studies have focused on developing high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved mechanical properties and corrosion resistance. The use of HEAs in fusion-reactor joints has shown promise, with some studies demonstrating enhanced strength and durability.
decision.unsolved: The development of a uniform W-Cu material with improved thermal transport and mechanical durability remains an open question. Current fabrication methods often result in phase separation, void formation, and defects, which can impair thermal transport and mechanical properties. Furthermore, the use of HEAs in fusion-reactor joints is still in its early stages, and more research is needed to fully understand their potential and limitations.
decision.lever: spark plasma sintering with optimized parameters
decision.why: Spark plasma sintering has shown promise in creating uniform W-Cu materials with improved mechanical properties. Optimizing the sintering parameters, such as temperature, pressure, and holding time, could help to minimize phase separation, void formation, and defects, leading to a more uniform and durable material. Additionally, the use of HEAs in fusion-reactor joints suggests that spark plasma sintering could be a viable method for creating these materials.
